title: Bulk File Editing with sed
markdown:
# Bulk File Editing with `sed`

In previous lab, `sed` output went to a new file using redirection — the original was never touched. That approach works for one-off transformations, but it doesn't scale. When a dozen configuration files all need the same hostname updated, writing individual redirects for each file is slow and error-prone. `sed` has a built-in solution: the `-i` flag edits files **in-place** — no temporary files, no redirects.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/sed-bulk.svg)

In this lab, we focus on three capabilities that make bulk editing practical: in-place substitution, line deletion, and applying the same changes to multiple files at once.

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Edit files directly in-place using `sed -i`
- Create automatic backups before editing with `sed -i.bak`
- Delete lines by pattern, blank lines, and comment lines
- Apply the same `sed` command to multiple files using a glob
- Chain multiple operations and use a sed script file for repeatable edits

## The Scenario: Preparing Configs for Release at `Poridhi.io`

The DevOps team is shipping a new release. Three service configuration files have been running with staging settings — staging hostnames, debug flags, blank lines, and developer comments. Before deploying to production, every config needs to be updated consistently:

1. All `staging` hostnames replaced with `prod`
2. Debug and log level settings removed
3. Comment lines and blank lines stripped out

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `deploylab/configs/api.conf` | API service configuration with staging values |
| `deploylab/configs/worker.conf` | Worker service configuration with staging values |
| `deploylab/configs/scheduler.conf` | Scheduler service configuration with staging values |

## Part 1: The `-i` Flag and How It Works

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/sed-sequence.svg)

In previous lab, `sed` output went to stdout and you redirected it:

```bash
sed 's/old/new/' file.conf > updated.conf   # writes to a new file
```

The `-i` flag changes this — `sed` writes the result back into the same file:

```bash
sed -i 's/old/new/' file.conf               # modifies file.conf directly
```
#### Safe Editing with Backups

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/sed-backup.svg)

When editing files in-place, mistakes can overwrite the original content. Use `-i.bak` when testing a new pattern — it saves the original as a backup file before making any changes:

```bash
sed -i.bak 's/old/new/' file.conf           # saves original as file.conf.bak
```

## Part 2: Setting Up the Environment

### Step 1: Create the Working Directory

```bash
mkdir -p deploylab/configs
```

### Step 2: Create the Config Files

```bash
cat > deploylab/configs/api.conf << 'EOF'
# Poridhi.io API Service Configuration
# Environment: staging

HOST=staging-host.poridhi.io
PORT=8080
DB_HOST=staging-db.poridhi.io
DB_PORT=5432
DEBUG=true
LOG_LEVEL=debug

CACHE_HOST=staging-cache.poridhi.io
CACHE_PORT=6379
MAX_CONNECTIONS=50
EOF
```

```bash
cat > deploylab/configs/worker.conf << 'EOF'
# Poridhi.io Worker Service Configuration
# Environment: staging

HOST=staging-host.poridhi.io
PORT=9000
DB_HOST=staging-db.poridhi.io
DB_PORT=5432
DEBUG=true
LOG_LEVEL=debug

QUEUE_HOST=staging-queue.poridhi.io
QUEUE_PORT=5672
WORKER_THREADS=4
EOF
```

```bash
cat > deploylab/configs/scheduler.conf << 'EOF'
# Poridhi.io Scheduler Service Configuration
# Environment: staging

HOST=staging-host.poridhi.io
PORT=9500
DB_HOST=staging-db.poridhi.io
DB_PORT=5432
DEBUG=true
LOG_LEVEL=debug

INTERVAL_SECONDS=30
MAX_RETRIES=3
EOF
```

Verify the files were created:

```bash
ls -l deploylab/configs/
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image.png)

Look at one file to confirm its contents:

```bash
cat deploylab/configs/api.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-1.png)

## Part 3: In-Place Substitution

### Step 1: Preview Before Editing

Before modifying any file in-place, run `sed` without `-i` first to confirm the output looks correct:

```bash
sed 's/staging/prod/g' deploylab/configs/api.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-2.png)

The `g` flag replaces all occurrences per line, not just the first. Here it updates every value that contains `staging` — hostnames, the environment comment, and the DB and cache hosts.

### Step 2: Edit In-Place

Once the output looks correct, apply it in-place:

```bash
sed -i 's/staging/prod/g' deploylab/configs/api.conf
cat deploylab/configs/api.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-3.png)

The file now contains `prod` throughout. No redirect, no new file — `api.conf` was modified directly.

### Step 3: Edit with a Backup

For `worker.conf`, create a backup before editing:

```bash
sed -i.bak 's/staging/prod/g' deploylab/configs/worker.conf
ls deploylab/configs/
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-4.png)

`worker.conf.bak` holds the original content. To see exactly what changed:

```bash
diff deploylab/configs/worker.conf.bak deploylab/configs/worker.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-5.png)

`diff` marks old lines with `<` and new lines with `>`.

> **Note:** Here, we can see that the `diff` command exited with status 1, which indicates that differences were found between the two files. This is the expected behavior of the `diff` command when comparing files that are not identical.

**Why it matters**: Always preview first. Use `-i.bak` when testing an unfamiliar pattern — the backup costs almost nothing and prevents having to recreate a file from scratch if something goes wrong.

## Part 4: Deleting Lines

`sed` deletes lines using the `d` command. The pattern before `d` selects which lines to remove. The pattern `sed '/pattern/d'` deletes every line where the pattern matches.

### Step 1: Delete Lines Matching a Pattern

Remove `DEBUG` and `LOG_LEVEL` settings from `api.conf`:

```bash
# Preview first
sed '/^DEBUG=/d; /^LOG_LEVEL=/d' deploylab/configs/api.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-6.png)

Apply in-place:

```bash
sed -i '/^DEBUG=/d; /^LOG_LEVEL=/d' deploylab/configs/api.conf
cat deploylab/configs/api.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-7.png)

`^DEBUG=` matches lines that **start with** `DEBUG=` — the `^` anchor prevents accidental matches if the string appears inside a value elsewhere in the file.

### Step 2: Delete Blank Lines

The file still has empty lines between sections. Remove them:

```bash
sed -i '/^$/d' deploylab/configs/api.conf
cat deploylab/configs/api.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-8.png)

`^$` matches lines that are empty from start (`^`) to end (`$`) — no characters between them.

### Step 3: Delete Comment Lines

Strip all lines that begin with `#`:

```bash
sed -i '/^#/d' deploylab/configs/api.conf
cat deploylab/configs/api.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-9.png)

`api.conf` now contains only key-value pairs — no comments, no blank lines, no debug settings. This is the clean format production config parsers expect.

**Why it matters**: Deleting by pattern is safer than deleting by line number. Deleting line 7 breaks the moment someone adds a line above it. Deleting `/^DEBUG=/` works correctly regardless of where the line appears.

## Part 5: Editing Multiple Files

At this point, `api.conf` is fully cleaned. `worker.conf` has `prod` values but still has debug settings, blank lines, and comments. `scheduler.conf` still has the original staging values from setup.

### Step 1: Apply a Change to All Matching Files

Pass a glob to `sed -i` to process all `.conf` files at once:

```bash
sed -i 's/staging/prod/g' deploylab/configs/*.conf
```

Verify all three files were updated:

```bash
grep "poridhi.io" deploylab/configs/*.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-10.png)

`grep` on multiple files prefixes each match with the filename — easy to confirm every file was updated and no staging values remain.

### Step 2: Chain Multiple Operations Across All Files

Clean up debug settings, blank lines, and comments in all files at once:

```bash
sed -i '/^DEBUG=/d; /^LOG_LEVEL=/d; /^$/d; /^#/d' deploylab/configs/*.conf
```

Verify the results:

```bash
cat deploylab/configs/worker.conf
cat deploylab/configs/scheduler.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-11.png)

Four operations applied to all three files in a single command.

### Step 3: Use a Sed Script File

When a command grows beyond two or three operations, inline semicolons become hard to read and maintain. Write the operations to a `.sed` script file and pass it with `-f`:

```bash
cat > deploylab/cleanup.sed << 'EOF'
s/staging/prod/g
/^DEBUG=/d
/^LOG_LEVEL=/d
/^$/d
/^#/d
EOF
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-12.png)

Create a fresh test config to demonstrate it:

```bash
cat > deploylab/configs/test.conf << 'EOF'
# Poridhi.io Test Service Configuration
# Environment: staging

HOST=staging-host.poridhi.io
PORT=7000
DB_HOST=staging-db.poridhi.io
DEBUG=true
LOG_LEVEL=debug

MAX_RETRIES=5
EOF
```

Apply all operations from the script file in one command:

```bash
sed -i -f deploylab/cleanup.sed deploylab/configs/test.conf
cat deploylab/configs/test.conf
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/a8a7470a65a39ff76bb28873c1d3b39bd4f29ad6/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2013/images/image-13.png)

`-f` reads operations from the file instead of the command line. All five operations — substitution plus four deletions — run in a single pass.

**Why it matters**: A sed script file is the standard way to manage complex, reusable sets of transformations. The same script can be version-controlled and applied to any number of files. Applying it to a hundred configs takes the same effort as applying it to one — this is what separates ad-hoc editing from a repeatable deployment process.

## Conclusion

In this lab, we extended `sed` from single-file output to a bulk editing tool:

- `-i` edits files directly without creating new files
- `-i.bak` saves the original as a backup before editing — use this when testing new patterns
- The `d` command deletes lines by pattern: matching content, blank lines, or comment markers
- Passing a glob (`*.conf`) to `sed -i` applies the same edit to every matching file at once
- A sed script file with `-f` packages multiple operations into a reusable, version-controllable artifact

`sed` is a stream-oriented tool that processes input line by line, so most commands scale from small files to very large ones without modification. While it typically does not load entire files into memory, certain commands can accumulate multiple lines, so memory usage depends on the script. Combined with glob expansion and script files, `sed` is a fast and scriptable tool for large-scale text processing and configuration management.
